analysis.investment_thesis: CESC is a classic slow-growing regulated utility — net profit has compounded at just 7.8% CAGR over nine years, operating income has actually declined at -1.6% CAGR, and at P/E 15.4x the PEG ratio is nearly 2.0x, meaning I'm paying a growth premium for a business that barely grows. Lynch's rule: never pay a PEG above 1.5 for a slow grower.
key_strengths: Highly predictable business with regulated tariffs — OCF positive 5/5 years, generating ₹2,500+ Cr annually
Renewable energy expansion (solar + wind hybrid projects totalling 1,500 MW) could provide genuine growth optionality over the next 5 years
Monopoly power distribution in Kolkata provides a captive customer base and stable base earnings
key_risks: Operating income 9Y CAGR of -1.6% — the core generation business is actually shrinking in profitability, masked by rising 'other income' which is non-recurring in nature
Debt/Equity of 1.41 is well above Lynch's 0.6 ceiling, and borrowings jumped from ₹14,544 Cr to ₹18,811 Cr in a single year as renewable capex accelerates
Free cash flow dropped sharply to ₹729 Cr in FY25 from ₹1,586 Cr in FY24, as capex surged to ₹1,863 Cr — capital intensity is rising just as returns on the core business stagnate
red_flags: PEG ratio of ~1.97 (P/E 15.4 / 7.8% net profit CAGR) — overvalued relative to its own growth rate; a utility should trade at a discount to growth, not a premium
Reliance on 'other income' growing at 34% CAGR (₹1,618 Cr in FY25) to prop up profits while operating income contracts is a quality concern
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I've always said that if you can't explain a stock's appeal in a few sentences, you probably shouldn't own it. CESC's pitch is: 'It's a stable regulated utility with some renewable upside.' That's fine — but stable and utility and regulated are three words that tell me I'm looking at a slow grower at best. Net profit grew from ₹1,309 Cr in FY20 to ₹1,428 Cr in FY25 — five years of capex, effort, and risk for 9% cumulative profit growth. That's not a compounder.

The renewable capex binge (CWIP jumped 5x to ₹890 Cr, capex doubled to ₹1,863 Cr in FY25) might bear fruit in 3-5 years, but you're paying for that optionality today at a P/E that doesn't give you a margin of safety. High leverage, declining operating margins in the core business, and PEG near 2x make this an avoid at current prices. If the stock fell 30-40% and the renewable projects came online, it might become interesting.
